newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Thousands seen marching for Belgian steel workers.
newsitem.headline: Thousands seen marching for Belgian steel workers.

text.p: BRUSSELS, Jan 31, Reuter - Thousands of demonstrators are expected to join aggrieved workers of bankrupt Belgian steel firm Forges de Clabecq SA in a mass protest on Sunday against job losses and company closures.
It was possible between 35,000 and 70,000 people would take part in the "March for Jobs" through the town of Tubize near Brussels where the steelworks is based, Belga news agency said.
A trade union spokeswoman told Reuters she was unable to give estimates of numbers yet.

Trade union organisers have called on everyone from workers to the unemployed, students and pensioners to join the march "against all closures and sackings, exclusion, misery and unemployment, and for social justice".

Clabecq was just one of 768 Belgian companies to go bankrupt this January alone, a record 36-percent leap from the same month in 1996, and at a cost of at least 4,800 jobs, Belgian trade and company data group Infotrade said on Friday.

Sunday's protest builds on the momentum of a noisy but peaceful protest in Brussels last Wednesday by 15,000 Belgian public sector workers angry about government plans to reform labour laws and expressing concern over pensions and privatisation.
The Clabecq rally will also be attended by parents caught in Belgium's paedophile and murder scandal.

They led a "White March" in Brussels last October of 250,000 people who wanted to show their support for paedophile victims' families and to call for judicial reform. The parents say they are now concerned for the welfare of Clabecq workers' families.

Since it was declared bankrupt by a Belgian commercial court on January 3 liquidators have been trying to salvage Clabecq - which has orders for the first quarter of 1997 - and save most of the 1,800 jobs at stake.

But Clabecq's majority shareholder and biggest creditor, Belgium's southern Walloon Region, last week turned down a request by the receivers for 800 million francs worth of financing, casting heavy doubt on the steelwork's future.
Saddled with high costs and low-grade products, the company had been struggling for months to survive in a cyclical, competitive industry weighed down by over-capacity.
Meanwhile Belgian banks are appealing a court ruling ordering them to extend credit lines worth 650 million Belgian francs to Clabecq for two months.

On Thursday Walloon Region president Robert Collignon said he still saw potential for Wallonia's biggest steel firm Cockerill Sambre to take over Clabecq's rolling mill - keeping up to 600 jobs - but this would be for Cockerill to decide.
In an interview with Le Soir newspaper he added that the region might also raise its guarantee for Clabecq's future operating losses to 250 million francs from 150 million.
But he made clear that Clabecq's survival was far from assured, saying "I am not at all certain work will resume".

Clabecq filed for bankruptcy in mid-December after the European Commission rejected a 1.5 billion Belgian franc ($47 million) rescue plan by the Walloon Region, which then withdrew its suppport for the firm.
